dotnet-11-runtime-async.title: .NET 11: runtime async
dotnet-11-runtime-async.shortDescription: No more compiler-generated state machines: fewer allocations and finally readable stack traces.

content.mainTitle: .NET 11: runtime async, the end of generated state machines
content.intro: Since C# 5, every async method is rewritten by the compiler into a state machine: a nested class, a state field, a MoveNext method. It works, but it costs allocations and pollutes every stack trace. .NET 11 moves that work into the runtime: the compiler emits a plain call and the VM handles suspension. Your source code does not change by a single line.
content.summary: Runtime async moves async suspension machinery from the compiler into the .NET 11 runtime: simpler IL, fewer allocations, readable stack traces.
tocItems: Pros and cons versus the classic async model

stateMachine.title: What the compiler generates today
stateMachine.description: Write a three-line async method and the compiler produces an entire class. It implements IAsyncStateMachine, stores progress in an integer field, and packs your whole method body into a MoveNext organized as a jump table.
costItems: A heap allocation as soon as the method actually suspends (boxing of the state struct)
Parasitic MoveNext frames in every call stack
Bulky IL, harder to inline and optimize
Unreadable generated names in profilers and memory dumps

whatChanges.title: What runtime async changes
whatChanges.description: With runtime async the compiler no longer emits a state class. It emits a direct call into the runtime, which handles suspension and resumption. The generated IL fits in a few instructions, and the JIT can optimize it like any other call.
gainsItems: Fewer allocations: the state struct is no longer systematically promoted to the heap
Much simpler IL, so more room for inlining
Since Preview 4, inlining also works at ReadyToRun compilation time through crossgen2
The .NET 11 runtime libraries now ship built with runtime-async=on

enable.title: Enabling and disabling
enable.description: The runtime libraries already benefit from it. For your own assemblies, opting in goes through an MSBuild property. Careful: the feature moved at every preview, so check the release notes of the preview you use.
enable.enableDescription: Target net11.0 and add the compiler feature. As of .NET 11 Preview 3, the RequiresPreviewFeatures attribute is no longer needed.
enable.disableDescription: If a profiler, an IL rewriter or a coverage tool is not compatible yet, you can turn the feature off at project level. Note that the DOTNET_RuntimeAsync environment switch was removed: there is no runtime opt-out anymore.

stackTraces.title: Readable stack traces
stackTraces.description: This is the most immediate benefit, and the one you notice on the very first production incident. Synthetic MoveNext frames disappear: the call stack finally looks like the methods you wrote.
stackTraces.note: In practice this also changes how logs and APM tools read: error grouping becomes more reliable, since it no longer relies on generated type names.

covariance.title: Task to Task<T> covariance
covariance.description: Another related .NET 11 addition: a derived method can now return Task<T> where the base method returns Task. The runtime generates the adapter needed for virtual dispatch to stay correct. That removes a good share of hand-written adaptation overloads.

useCases.title: Concrete use cases
useCases.description: Runtime async requires no rewrite. Heavily asynchronous workloads are the ones that benefit most.
items: High-throughput ASP.NET Core APIs: every request crosses dozens of async methods, and saved allocations add up
Workers and queue consumers: long processing loops where GC pressure is the limiting factor
Widely reused libraries: recompiling your library with runtime-async benefits every caller
Incident diagnosis: usable call stacks without mentally decoding generated names
Tail-latency sensitive applications: fewer gen0 collections triggered by state machines

comparison.title: Pros and cons versus the classic async model
comparison.description: The comparison point is the current model: the compiler-generated state machine, battle-tested since C# 5 and present in every .NET runtime up to and including .NET 10.
prosItems: No source change: your async and await stay identical
Fewer allocations and reduced GC pressure on heavily asynchronous paths
Stack traces and memory profiles finally readable
Inlining possible all the way into ReadyToRun compilation
Enabled by default in the .NET 11 runtime libraries
consItems: Requires .NET 11, which is not an LTS release, with GA on November 10, 2026
Real gains only show up once the whole call graph is recompiled
Tools that rewrite IL (AOP, instrumentation, code coverage) may need an update
Some profilers and APM agents must be validated before a production switch
No environment switch to roll back at runtime anymore: the decision is made at compile time
Your baseline benchmarks need to be redone: published numbers do not apply to your workload
comparison.verdict: In practice: enable runtime async on a non-critical service first, compare allocations and tail latency before and after, and validate your observability chain. The gain is real but gradual, while the risk sits entirely in the tooling.
